title: How to tell if a LinkedIn profile is fake
summary: A polished profile proves little. How to read a profile's age, badges, history and photo, look for the person outside LinkedIn, and weigh what each check is…
body_markdown:
Check its history before its polish. Look at when the profile was created and what its verifications prove, read the work history for details that can be checked, run the photo through a reverse image search, and look for the person outside LinkedIn in records other people wrote over the years. No single sign settles it, so confirm anything important through the employer or another channel you found yourself.


Usually not by eye. In a 2022 study published in PNAS, people sorted AI-generated faces from real ones with 48.2 percent accuracy, close to chance, and familiar tells such as eyes centred in the frame belong to older generators. A reverse image search is more useful: a match under a different name, on pages older than the profile, points to a stolen photo, while no match fits a generated face and a real person whose photo is not posted elsewhere equally well.


Yes. An identity badge shows that one of LinkedIn's verification partners checked a government ID and that LinkedIn matched it to the profile's name, and a workplace badge shows the member confirmed their association with a company, for example through a work email. Neither shows that the rest of the history or the photo is real, or who is using the account today, though LinkedIn is testing a newer badge for experience that connections confirm. A missing badge proves little, because verification is optional and not offered everywhere.


Open the profile, click More and choose About this member (earlier called About this profile). LinkedIn introduced the panel in 2022 to show when a profile was created and last updated, and verifications are listed there too. A recent creation date is not evidence of fraud on its own, but it means the profile cannot vouch for a long career by itself.


Find the company's careers page yourself, check how it says its recruiters contact candidates, and see whether the recruiter has a workplace verification and is connected to colleagues at that company. Be wary of unexpected offers with unusually high pay, requests to move to another messaging app and requests to run code as a test, which the FBI lists among its warning signs, and never pay or hand over account credentials to apply. If in doubt, contact the company through its own website.


Open the profile, click More, then Report / Block, and select Report \[name\] or entire account. Select This person is impersonating someone or This account is not a real person, then submit the report. LinkedIn says reported members won't know who made the report.
